planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade in spring; this circumboreal oak fern relative needs cool, moist conditions and resents hot, dry summers.

directions: Plant divisions in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, mimicking the boreal and subalpine conifer forests of its native Japan, Korea, far-eastern Russia, and parts of northwestern North America. Jesso oak fern closely resembles the more familiar Gymnocarpium dryopteris but holds slightly narrower, more finely cut triangular blades on wiry black-green stalks, spreading gradually by slender rhizomes into a low, airy groundcover. It is best suited to cool-summer rock gardens, alpine troughs, and northern woodland plantings where summer heat and humidity are moderate, and pairs naturally with mosses, dwarf dogwoods, and other boreal understory companions. Give it steady moisture and shelter from wind and strong sun for best performance.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil over rocky or talus substrate in full to partial shade; this Appalachian endemic favors cool, shaded sandstone and shale outcrops and ravines.

directions: Site in moist, humus-rich soil with good drainage over rocky or talus substrate in full to partial shade, recreating the cool sandstone and shale ravines of the central and southern Appalachian Mountains where this diploid segregate of the oak fern complex is endemic. It closely resembles common oak fern (Gymnocarpium dryopteris) in its delicate, horizontally held, triangular fronds on slender black stipes, differing mainly in subtler technical characters of pinnule shape and chromosome number rather than obvious garden appearance. Because it is uncommon in the nursery trade, it is best obtained through native plant society rescues or specialist fern growers rather than general retail sources, and is most appropriate for native-plant and rock garden collections in its home range. Keep it consistently cool and moist; it does not tolerate hot, dry summer sites.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants into rock crevices or well-drained, humus-thin soil in partial to full shade in fall, mimicking the cliff ledges and rocky slopes of the western mountains where it grows; it goes summer-dormant in dry seasons and resumes growth with fall and winter moisture.

directions: Tuck divisions into rocky crevices, dry-laid stone walls, or thin, well-drained soil pockets in partial to full shade, recreating the cliff faces, talus slopes, and rock outcrops across the western mountains and intermountain West where this drought-deciduous polypody naturally grows. Fronds are small, once-pinnate, and leathery, emerging with fall and winter moisture and curling up or dying back in the dry heat of summer, a natural dormancy strategy rather than a sign of decline. It is ideal for naturalistic rock gardens, retaining walls, and native plant collections in dry-summer climates, requiring minimal supplemental water once established on an appropriate rocky site. Avoid rich garden soil and summer irrigation, which encourage rot rather than growth.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil or rock crevices in partial to full shade in fall; this evergreen European polypody tolerates both tree bark and stone walls, needing only moderate moisture once established.

directions: Plant in humus-rich but well-drained soil, old stone walls, or on mossy tree trunks in partial to full shade; intermediate polypody is a naturally occurring fertile species arising from hybridization between common polypody and southern polypody, widespread across the hedgerows, wall tops, and woodlands of Britain and western Europe. Its evergreen, once-pinnate, leathery dark green fronds are somewhat broader and more robust than common polypody, and it tolerates considerably more lime and alkalinity in the soil. It is an excellent, low-maintenance evergreen groundcover or wall fern for cool, maritime-influenced shade gardens, requiring little care beyond protection from prolonged summer drought. It combines well with hart's-tongue fern and other calcicole woodland species.

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants after all frost danger has passed into warm, humid, consistently moist soil near a trellis, fence, or shrub in partial shade; this tropical climbing fern needs sustained warmth and humidity to thrive.

directions: Plant at the base of a trellis, fence, or open shrub in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade with high ambient humidity; Asian climbing fern produces twining, vine-like fronds with a persistently elongating rachis that can climb 10 to 25 feet, scrambling over supports with finely divided, fan-lobed pinnae unlike any true vine. Native to tropical and subtropical Asia and the Pacific Islands, where its tough fibers are traditionally woven into mats, hats, and baskets, it is grown ornamentally in warm, humid gardens as a distinctive screening or trellis fern. It requires frost-free, humid, tropical to warm-subtropical conditions and will not survive outdoors where temperatures approach freezing. Provide sturdy support and consistent moisture for best climbing performance.
sources: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; this Florida and Gulf Coast native maiden fern thrives at swamp margins and in wet hammocks and is not reliably cold-hardy north of its subtropical range.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade at the margins of ponds, swamps, and wet hammocks, mirroring the native habitat of this low-growing maiden fern across Florida, the West Indies, and Mexico into Central America. Its pinnate-pinnatifid, light green fronds carry tiny resinous dots on the lower surface -- the source of both its common and scientific names -- and it stays evergreen in consistently warm, humid, frost-free sites. It spreads gradually to form a low colony and is well suited to subtropical rain gardens, bog garden margins, and naturalistic wet-shade plantings in its hardiness range. It is not frost-hardy and should be treated as an annual or container plant outside USDA zones 9 through 11.

planting.note: Mount or plant divisions after frost danger has passed on tree trunks, in limestone crevices, or in loose, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; long strap fern wants constant humidity and does not tolerate freezing temperatures.

directions: Grow on tree trunks, in limestone or coquina rock crevices, or in loose, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade with steady humidity, matching the hammocks and swamp edges of Florida, the Caribbean, and tropical Central and South America where this fern grows as an epiphyte or epipetric plant. Unlike most shade ferns, its fronds are simple and undivided -- long, glossy, strap-shaped, and leathery, arching gracefully from a short creeping rhizome to create a bold, architectural accent among finely cut companion ferns. It is a popular landscape and container fern in subtropical Florida gardens, often mounted on oaks or palms, but is strictly frost-tender and must be grown as a protected container specimen outside USDA zones 9 through 11. Keep humidity high and avoid letting the rhizome dry out completely.
